title: File and Directory Permissions Modification
summary: File and directory permissions modification covers the deliberate rewriting of access control rules so that an adversary gains rights the operating system would otherwise refuse. Every mainstream platform expresses these rules differently, but the shape of the abuse is consistent: the attacker either grants themselves access to an object they cannot currently touch, or removes access from others so that defenders cannot read, replace or clean the file. Because permissions are enforced by the kernel and checked on every access, an adversary does not need to defeat security software at all; they simply become a legitimate user of the object according to the rules the system itself consults. This is rarely an end in itself. It is an enabling step that appears in the chain before persistence through an existing executable or script, before the hijacking of a trusted binary or configuration file that loads during normal use, and before the deletion or encryption of data during an impact phase. The behaviour is also common and benign, because administrators and installers adjust permissions constantly, so context carries the detection. Useful signals are the combination of a permission change with a sensitive or unusual target, an actor whose role does not include administration, a burst of recursive changes across many paths in a short period, and the follow-on action that the changed permission made possible. Audit policy must be switched on for object access before any of this is visible, and the recorded events should be joined to the process creation record that shows which utility and which command line caused the change.

beginner.definition: Files and folders have rules that say who may read, change or run them. These rules are called permissions. Attackers change the rules so they can reach files that were closed to them, or so that other people cannot reach them.
beginner.whyItMatters: The computer enforces these rules itself, so an attacker who edits them is not breaking in. They are simply using the file within the rules as the system now understands them. This step usually comes before something worse, such as planting a program that starts automatically. It can also lock out the people trying to investigate or clean up after an incident. Because administrators change permissions all the time for valid reasons, the meaning depends on which file was changed and who changed it.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a file or folder they cannot read, change or run with their current account.
They check who currently owns it and what rights their account has been given.
If needed they take ownership, which is a deliberate change of who controls the object.
On Windows this is usually done with built-in commands that edit access lists in bulk.
On Linux and Mac systems the same result comes from changing the owner or the access mode.
The changed rule lets them read, replace or delete the file, or blocks others from doing so.
beginner.example: Picture a shared office fridge where every shelf has a label with the name of the team allowed to use it. Nobody steals from the fridge; people only take what their label allows. Now imagine someone peels off a label and writes their own name on the shelf, or removes the label of another team. Nothing is forced open. The rule was rewritten, and from that moment the fridge itself hands over the contents to the wrong person.
takeaways: Permission changes are an enabler, so always ask what happened next.
Turn on object access auditing, or the change itself is never recorded.
Take ownership is a deliberate act and rarely needed in normal daily work.

objectives: Explain what an access control list is and how the system uses it to allow or deny access.
Describe how taking ownership of an object differs from being granted access to it.
Give examples of later techniques that depend on changing permissions first.
Explain why benign administrative permission changes make context essential for detection.
Identify the auditing prerequisites needed to observe permission changes at all.
